travelAdvisory.summary:
Updated to include a risk indicator for health and to reflect additional safety and security information.
Do Not Travel to:

Kenya-Somalia border counties (Garissa, Wajir, Mandera), Tana River County, and coastal areas north of Malindi due to terrorism and kidnapping;
West Pokot and western Turkana County due to banditry;
Parts of Marsabit and Turkana Counties within 30 miles (50 kilometers) of the Ethiopian border due to cross-border incursions.

Reconsider Travel to:

The Nairobi neighborhoods

healthcare.summary: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to Kenya. Emergency numbers (999), yellow fever vaccination required, pharmacy tips, restricted medications, malaria precautions, and travel insurance advice.

required: Yellow Fever (required for all travelers over 1 year of age; must have valid certificate)
recommended: Meningococcal meningitis (for travel during dry season, especially in the north)
Rabies (for animal exposure, especially dogs and wildlife)
Malaria prophylaxis (essential for most of Kenya)
vaccinations.notes: Yellow fever vaccination is required for ALL travelers entering Kenya — must present valid certificate. Malaria prophylaxis is strongly recommended for most of the country, especially during rainy seasons. Nairobi at altitude has lower malaria risk but prophylaxis is still recommended for travel to game parks.

pharmacy.hours: Most pharmacies open 8am-10pm; some 24-hour pharmacies in Nairobi and Mombasa; chains include Pharmácia Kenya, Nairobi Women's Hospital Pharmacy, and independent pharmacies
pharmacy.tips: Many medications available OTC. Pharmacists are helpful. Bring a list of medications with generic names. Malaria prophylaxis is essential — bring your preferred brand as availability varies. In rural areas, pharmacy access is very limited — bring all medications you may need.

water.notes: Tap water is NOT safe to drink in Kenya. Use bottled or filtered water at all times. Avoid ice in drinks outside of hotels and reputable restaurants. Bottled water is cheap and widely available — use it exclusively for drinking and brushing teeth. Waterborne diseases are common.

healthcare.foodSafetyTips: Be cautious with food from street vendors and small eateries. In hotels, lodges, and reputable restaurants, food is generally safe. Avoid raw salads and uncooked vegetables outside of upscale establishments. In safari lodges and coastal resorts, food standards are high. Stick to well-cooked foods served hot.

travelInsurance.requiredNote: Required for visa on arrival / e-visa — must show proof of travel insurance with medical evacuation coverage.
travelInsurance.tips: Travel insurance with medical evacuation coverage is mandatory for entry and essential. Public hospitals have limited resources; serious cases require evacuation to Nairobi private hospitals or medical evacuation to South Africa or Europe ($10,000-50,000+). Ensure coverage includes safari activities, helicopter evacuation, and malaria treatment.

healthcare.qualityNotes: Private hospitals in Nairobi and Mombasa offer good quality care comparable to regional standards. Public hospitals are overcrowded and under-resourced. Rural areas have very limited medical facilities — serious cases require evacuation to Nairobi or abroad. Pharmacies widely available in cities.

medications.prescriptionRules: A prescription is required for prescription medications but enforcement varies. Antibiotics and many drugs available OTC. Carry all medications in original packaging with a doctor's note.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD stimulant medications (Adderall, Ritalin, Vyvanse)
restrictedMeds.note: Stimulants are controlled substances. Bring original prescription, doctor's letter, and only the amount needed. Declare at customs.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine is controlled. Carry alternatives if possible.

restrictedMeds.name: Psychotropic medications (diazepam, alprazolam, etc.)
restrictedMeds.note: Benzodiazepines require documentation. Carry a doctor's letter explaining medical necessity.

restrictedMeds.name: Narcotics (morphine, tramadol, etc.)
restrictedMeds.note: Strong narcotics require strict documentation. Carry alternatives or minimal quantities with documentation.

medications.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter listing all medications with generic names. Keep medications in original packaging. For controlled substances, carry original prescriptions and a note explaining medical necessity. Yellow fever certificate required for entry from endemic countries.
medications.generalAdvice: Kenya requires travelers to carry prescription medications in original containers with a doctor's letter. Controlled substances need documentation from your home country, and some medications available OTC elsewhere require a prescription in Kenya. Drug trafficking carries severe penalties including life imprisonment.

controlledSubstances.note: Illegal for recreational use. Possession can result in heavy fines or imprisonment. Bhang (cannabis drink) is culturally present but still technically illegal.
Available by prescription only. Travelers should carry original containers and a doctor's letter. Import of large quantities requires advance approval.
Controlled substances requiring a valid prescription and supporting documentation. Carry a doctor's letter explaining the medical need.
Prescription-only. Carry original packaging and a doctor's certificate. Available locally with a Kenyan prescription.
Legal and widely available in Kenya, but illegal in many other countries. Do not attempt to export khat when leaving.
Strictly illegal. Drug trafficking in Kenya carries penalties up to life imprisonment.

scams.name: Safari Price Gouging
scams.description: Unlicensed operators offer cheap safaris then demand extra fees or provide substandard vehicles.
scams.avoidance: Book with KATO-registered operators. Get full pricing in writing.

scams.name: Matatu Pickpocketing
scams.description: Pickpockets operate on crowded matatus, especially CBD routes.
scams.avoidance: Keep valuables in front pockets. Use ride-sharing apps for longer trips.

scams.name: Fake M-Pesa Agents
scams.description: Scammers pose as M-Pesa agents asking for test payments or your PIN.
scams.avoidance: Only use official Safaricom shops. Never share your PIN.

connectivity.simOptions: Safaricom (M-Pesa network) prepaid SIM at JKIA airport or any Safaricom shop. Need passport. Data is cheap. M-Pesa mobile money is essential.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Good WiFi at hotels and cafes in Nairobi and Mombasa. Limited in safari parks and rural areas. Some lodges have WiFi.
connectivity.bestOption: Safaricom prepaid SIM — essential for M-Pesa mobile payments (widely used for everything). Buy at airport on arrival.

cultural.tipping: 10% at restaurants. Safari guides/drivers: $15-25/day per person. Hotel porters: KES 200-500.
cultural.dressCode: Modest dress in rural and coastal areas (Muslim regions). Safari: neutral colors. Nairobi is more cosmopolitan and casual.
cultural.greetings: 'Jambo' or 'Habari yako' (how are you). Handshake is standard. Elders and authority figures addressed with respect.
taboos: Photographing people without asking (especially Maasai — negotiate a fee)
Pointing at wildlife during safari (use open hand)
Disrespecting the flag or national symbols
cultural.haggling: Expected at markets, souvenir shops, matatus (minibuses), and with taxi drivers. Not at supermarkets. Start at 40-50% of asking price.

safety.lgbtSafety: Kenya criminalizes same-sex relations with penalties of up to 14 years imprisonment, though enforcement is inconsistent. LGBTQ+ travelers should exercise extreme discretion. Public displays of affection between same-sex couples are not safe anywhere in the country.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Solo female travel is possible with careful planning. Stick to established safari operators and tourist areas. Nairobi requires extra caution — avoid walking alone at night. Coastal areas like Mombasa and Diani are generally safer for tourists but harassment can occur.
safety.notes: Kenya is a popular tourist destination with well-established safari and beach tourism infrastructure. However, crime is a real concern in Nairobi (especially Eastlands) and parts of Mombasa. Use reputable tour operators, avoid the Somali border region, and don't walk with valuables. Most safari experiences and national parks are very safe.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: e-Visa required ($50). Apply online before travel. Some nationalities eligible for visa on arrival. ETA system being implemented.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: January-March (hot, dry — good for safari). July-October (Great Migration in Masai Mara). June-October dry season overall best.

hospitals.name: Aga Khan University Hospital Nairobi
hospitals.notes: Best hospital in East Africa for tourists. English-speaking staff, international patient services.

hospitals.name: Nairobi Hospital
hospitals.notes: Good private hospital with solid emergency facilities.

immediate: Avoid river banks and low-lying areas during heavy rain
Do not attempt to cross flooded roads on foot or by vehicle
Move to higher ground if in flood-prone area
Follow Kenya Red Cross and local authority alerts
after: Avoid contact with floodwater — leptospirosis and cholera risk
Boil or purify drinking water after floods

steps: File a police report immediately — get the report number, you will need it
Contact the US Embassy or nearest consulate: Contact the nearest US Embassy
Bring the police report + any ID you have (driver's license, copy of passport)
Apply for an Emergency Passport (usually issued within 1-2 business days)
Notify your travel insurance and airline of the situation
stolenPassport.notes: Keep a digital copy of your passport in cloud storage (Google Photos, iCloud) and email yourself a scan before travel.

steps: Go to the nearest police station (or call 999)
Bring ID or a copy of your passport if available
Request a written report — ask for an English copy or certified translation if needed
Keep the report number safe — required for insurance claims
For theft: list all stolen items with approximate values
policeReport.notes: In many countries, tourist police stations are available in major cities — they have English-speaking staff. Ask your hotel concierge for the nearest tourist police.

steps: If involved in an accident: do not move vehicles if anyone is injured
Call police (999) and ambulance (999) if there are injuries
Exchange contact, license, and insurance details with other parties
Document the scene with photos before moving vehicles
Contact your rental car company's emergency line
Contact your travel insurance's 24h assistance line
roadsideAssistance.notes: Traffic drives on the LEFT. An International Driving Permit (IDP) is required for most foreign licenses. Rental vehicles are available at major airports and cities.
